title: A moving calendar
hookLine: a lunar year is about eleven days shorter, so Ramadan visits every season over thirty-three years
tomorrow: Who feeds me and heals me

cards: Two cousins, years apart in age, can remember childhood Ramadans in different seasons. One remembers long summer days, the fast running late into the evening, playing outside in the heat with a dry mouth.

The other remembers short winter fasts, breaking it before the early dark, homework at the table afterward. Same month, same rules, a completely different experience. That's not a change in the religion.
It's the calendar, doing exactly what it was built to do.

teach.b: The Hijri calendar follows the moon. Each month begins when the new crescent, the hilal, is seen or reckoned.
Twelve lunar months add up to about three hundred fifty-four days, roughly eleven days shorter than the solar year.

So every year Ramadan arrives about eleven days earlier by the solar calendar, and over roughly thirty-three years it slides backward through every season and comes round again. The Qur'an names this rhythm.
In Surah Al-Baqarah people ask about the new moons, and the answer is that they are markers of time for people and for the pilgrimage.

Surah At-Tawbah says the number of months with God is twelve, and criticizes the practice called nasi', postponing a month; some historians understand that as an older Arabian habit of adding a month so the year kept step with the seasons, while others read it as shifting a sacred month.
The Qur'anic calendar lets the months move. Here's what that does. Nobody's Ramadan is always the hard one, or always the easy one.
Over a lifetime, someone in the far north gets long summer fasts and short winter ones, and when the north has its long fasts, the south has its short ones. Hajj travels through the seasons too.
And the moon is something anyone can see, from a roof or a field, without a printed calendar.

These two weeks of holy days move with it: the Hijri new year, 'Ashura's two memories, Mawlid, the night journey, Sha'ban's getting ready, Ramadan's book and seclusion and khatm, the takbir of Eid, six more, the ten days, and the feast of the sacrifice.
Every one of them drifts through the seasons, together. Tomorrow, back to the book, and the middle of the Qur'an.

how: Muslims date Ramadan, Hajj and the other holy days by the lunar Hijri calendar, beginning months by sighting or calculating the new crescent, so the festivals move about eleven days earlier each solar year.

games.q: you're planning your life around Ramadan, and someone suggests adding a month now and then so it always lands in winter. what does the Qur'anic calendar do?

lets the months move through the seasons.

games.why: Surah At-Tawbah criticizes nasi', postponing a month; the Hijri months move freely, so Ramadan visits every season.

practice: Look out the window, or picture it: what season is it where you are, and is it a season of long days or short ones?
Then let your mind run thirty-three years forward, when the same month will have visited every one of those seasons. If you pray, you can hold that thought as a quiet hope.
